content: Six out of ten unintended pregnancies and three out of ten total pregnancies result in induced abortion. When abortion is performed safely—defined as using a method recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), appropriate to the gestational age, and carried out by a skilled provider—the associated risks are minimal. However, 4% of abortions are categorized as least safe, posing significant health risks. Unsafe abortion is a critical public health and human rights issue, disproportionately affecting individuals in developing countries and those in vulnerable or marginalized situations. In countries where abortion is highly restricted by law or inaccessible due to other barriers, safe abortion often becomes a privilege of wealthier individuals. Poorer women are frequently forced to seek services from unskilled providers in unsafe conditions or attempt self-induced abortions using unsafe methods. These practices lead to preventable deaths and morbidities, which place a burden on public health systems and violate women's human rights. The legal status of abortion does not influence the likelihood of a woman seeking an abortion but significantly impacts her access to safe abortion services. Unsafe abortions account for approximately 2% of all maternal deaths, equating to an estimated 13,865 to 38,940 lives lost annually, with many more experiencing severe health complications. Developing countries bear 97% of the global burden of unsafe abortions, with the highest proportions occurring in regions with restrictive abortion laws. Abortion, when performed using medication or a simple outpatient surgical procedure, is a safe healthcare intervention if conducted with methods appropriate to the gestational age and by a trained provider. Complications or serious adverse effects are rare under these circumstances. Medical abortion has revolutionized access to quality abortion care globally, enabling individuals to safely self-manage the process during the first 12 weeks of gestation, provided they have access to accurate information and support from trained health workers if needed. Service delivery models with minimal medical supervision can improve access, particularly in restricted or crisis settings, while maintaining safety and effectiveness. Despite these advancements, legal, policy, and practical barriers continue to hinder access to quality abortion care in both lowand high-resource settings. Comprehensive abortion care includes accurate information, abortion management (including care for pregnancy loss or spontaneous abortion), and post-abortion care. WHO guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to ensure global access to quality abortion care. These guidelines integrate human rights principles, addressing the underlying determinants of health and promoting gender equality. The guidelines emphasize equity, inclusivity, and people-centered care, recognizing the diverse needs of individuals seeking abortion services. They advocate for integrating abortion care with other sexual and reproductive health services, such as HIV and STI testing and treatment, and family planning. Services must be accessible, youth-friendly, and welcoming to all, including sexual and gender minorities, individuals with disabilities, and marginalized groups. Providers must ensure non-discriminatory care, respecting the dignity, autonomy, and preferences of all individuals. An enabling environment is essential for quality abortion care. This includes respect for human rights, supportive legal and policy frameworks, accessible information, and a well-functioning health system. Countries must ratify international human rights treaties addressing sexual and reproductive health, implement laws and policies promoting these rights, and establish mechanisms to monitor and address barriers to care. Policies should also aim to reduce unintended pregnancies by providing quality contraceptive services. The WHO guidelines consolidate and update previous recommendations, reflecting recent changes in abortion care practices. They address legal and policy considerations, clinical care, service delivery, and emerging research priorities. The guidelines are intended for policymakers, healthcare providers, and stakeholders to ensure evidence-based, quality abortion care is available and accessible globally.
